name: Adam
comments:
Conditions were not great on 20m this afternoon. I could just hear DJ9FM, Willie, but alas, he did not hear me. Maybe I need to peddle harder? 

To top off the poor conditions on 20m we had a storm pass through just before the NET. I thought it was done and dusted, sadly, it was slow moving and another was following behind, causing significant static crashes. 

All was not lost! I did work Phil ZL1PB who had a solid signal. He was no match for the crashes though and I had to cut the QSO short to unplug the antenna(s).

Cheers
Adam, VK4IM

name: Willie
qth: JO30WJ - Montabaur - Half way between Frankfurt in the south and Cologne in the north.
heardOther: myself on ironstonefarm SDR with s5 ;)
comments:
I wanted to do better than the last times and so I took my car to a nearby top of a small hill. Here I set up my gear in a misty and early morning. Outside of the car there was a self build drive-on mount for my mast carrying a 1/4 wave vertical with elevated radials. In the car were the Yaesu 897, my homebrew key, a headphone, batteries and a notebook.
The temperature was ok, as soon as I got inside the car and out of the wind. Then I started calling CQ.

My CQ VK QRS was answered by a station from Belarus, EW3DI, but he was gone before we could exchange reports. The next one was from Russia R2WB. We exchanged reports and I told him, that I was looking for VK.

When ZL1PB called, I first understood DL1... quite common here ;) ... but then, RR, I got it. There still was QRM and QSB, hard conditions for a beginner like me. But we managed to get a valid QSO. Now I am very pleased, that I had the first QSO in the group.
caption: Portable set up in the morning mist.

name: Lance
comments:
I didn't manage much time on the air on Tuesday, so was fortunate to catch Mark, 2KI, for a brief ragchew at the start of the evening.

Having checked the space weather forecast and noted the solar flux under 100, I wasn't expecting too many stations to make it down to southern Tas.  Thus anticipating a quite band I elected to use my old TS-520S which has no CW filters.  How wrong I was.  A low SFI (Solar Flux Index) does of course result in lower signal strengths, but also lower QRN resulting in an improved SNR.  I couldn't tune anywhere in the vicinity of our COA without a few stations operating in my passband, both local (VK/ZL) and many VA stations.  It was a good opportunity to exercise that filter between my ears, as well as trying to copy two stations at the same time.
caption: My trusty TS-520S.  A beautiful rig to operate, but the lack of narrow filters can be a challenge on a busy band.

name: Mark
qth: camping at Bermagui on the South Coast of NSW
heard40: VK3WOW, VK3XU, VK2TI, ZL3XDJ, VK3TBR, VK4PN, VK6NW
heardOther: ZL1PB@20, DJ9FM@20, VK4IM@20, VK6RR@20, IU4FLS@20, VK3ACU@160, VK2BJ@160
comments:
15m

Well well - despite predictions of depressed conditions on Tuesday, I had fun.

We were still at Bermagui as it turned out - some administrative things going on that meant our plan to head outside of phone and internet coverage had to be shelved for a few days.  So that afternoon, I put my ZS6BKW doublet back up at 5m, after taking it down earlier in the week due to the prediction of storms.

At the designated sked slot I tried 15m, calling and listening for Edi DO2EMR at Stuttgart;  my old TS-120S transceiver at home refuses to work above 15m (another repair job on the long list for me) so it was nice to be able to give 15m a go on my FT-817.  Unfortunately, nil from Edi this week - and in fact, there was nothing going on down the CW end of the band at that time.

20m

20m was apparently performing per the depressed conditions as well.  

I could hear Phil ZL1PB at Tauranga chatting to Willie DJ9FM at Holler, but Willie was very very weak.  More like the background noise blending into tones rather than definable dits and dahs;  certainly not enough to copy any form of callsign.  I also heard Adam VK4IM and Roy VK6RR calling.  At the sked time, I slipped over to Fausto IU4FLS's frequency, and again, I could hear the noise synchronising into vague tones, but not enough of Fausto to make out any characters.

40m

40m wasn't suffering from the depressed conditions.  There was a bunch of DX stations coming through when I started listening at 0600z - they were all too fast for me, but it sounded like the band was open to Europe -  I caught what sounded like German callsigns among the piles of stations.

A CQ call or two resulted in a call from El Editore, Lance VK7TO at Margate;  Lance was bending the needle here, a solid RSN 598.  The N-8 was due to the charger on my AVan's Lithium deep cycle battery doing it's one-per-second thing - luckily on fast AGC, the noise was S0 between bursts with my CW filter in - without the filter, the noise was about S9 on bursts and S8 between.  Lance annpounced his arrival with a short burst of carrier while he peaked the drive control (if it was one of his classic Kenwood transceivers) or pre-select control if it was his Yaesu transceiver.  Used to be par for the course to hear this.... the operator would tune up somewhere quietly, but when moving around the band, a quick peak-up was needed... thanks for the little nostalgia Lance.  As normal, we talked about the weather and CW filters.

After 20m I came back to 40 and chatted to Wimal VK1WA up at Bonner, Georg VK2DLF at St Marys.  After dinner I came back and was pleased to chat again to one of our newer family members, Jamie VK3IDK at Point Cook.

I listened in to Manny VK3DRQ at Blackburn chatting to Wayne VK6NW at Bridgetown - really nice signal from both... 40m was certainly strutting its stuff across the country this week.  I'm wondering whether I need to put up a ZS6BKW doublet at home to complement my 80m double-extended Zepp - hmmm.  I caught Manny after his QSO, but conditions were changing and our ancient mariner was struggling to copy my 10,000mW.

40m had pretty much done its dash across the nation, and strong signals were rolling in from the States and from South East Asia;  time for me to high-tail to 80m.

80m

I tried calling on 80m, and could hear myself on the Hoddys Well KiwiSDR near Northam WA, but there wasn't much going on in the West when I listened.  After announcing myself on our CQQRS WhatsApp Alerts, Peter VK6NQL came up;  Peter had a very good RSN 488 signal, but just couldn't pick put enough of my QRP signal to make a go of it.  

After more CQs, it was getting pretty late over this way, and I decided to head off to bed.  A last quick check of the WA SDR.... sure enough there was a trace 1kHz above mine.... one click and I was listening to Derek VK4DRK at Toowoomba rolling in RSN 598;  narrow filters can be great... but I had no idea that he was there, bing outside my passband;  luckily I picked him up on the waterfall display in WA.  I had chatted to Derek three weeks ago, but hadn't done so for more than 18 months before then;  great that he was able to have a go on 80m again like we used to in the old days of the CQQRS net.  We had a nice chat about his gear - his Kenwood TS-570S was doing a good job into his End-Fed Half-Wave... and the weather - over 100mm of rain there!

160m

The other advantage of using my trusty FT-817 was that it covered 160m.  Jordan VK3ACU at Meredith advertised on the CQQRS WhatsApp Alerts that he was calling on 1825kHz.  He was a nice RSN 588 with me, as was VK2BJ in Sydney;  however, I couldn't participate because neither my antenna nor my coupler had enough mojo to work on Top Band.

Through the whole net I was trying to make the little YA1860 key generate some sort of rhythm.  The contact gap was too wide, and the spring tension was a little high... and adding to the challenge, there's a second set of contacts that close before the main contacts, and increase the load a tad.  The result is a rather staccato keying, where the dot lengths are a bit shorter than I'd like.  I didn't have tools to adjust the gap (there's no tension screw in my key any more) so I was trying different positions.  Sometimes holding a spare finger of the off-hand under the back of the mechanism helped a bit (by closing the gap a tad and perhaps offsetting the tension), and a cutting board on my leg also helped.  But I found over all, the best keying actually happened when I held the key on my leg with the base plate tangential to the leg, and keying sideways!  I couldn't get a picture of that position.... one hand too few!

 So, in all - a good fun night for me on the lower bands;  thank you to everyone who was on.
caption: YA1860 Key - Trying to Find A Rhythm.

name: Paul
worked40: Zl1pb, zl1ts, vk3mj, vk5ao, vk3acu, vk7ta, vk7jz.
comments:
The radio I  used on 40m this net was my ft901D.  

For any readers interested , today's work on this rig before the net involved swapping out the 40+ year old audio driver transistors 2sc100gr to new ksc1845fta.  These are very low noise NPN units specifically designed for audio drivers.  I have found if your prepared to do enough  soldering old sets can often benefit by upgrading and replacing the silicon transistors. HIFI restorers also do this as a mater of course to get premium performance.

  If you notice some slight chirp on my cw signal from the ft901d,  it may be i have engaged the rit control to net in your signal.  The ft901 series did this from factory it uses a vari cap diode for rit and has a small .33uf cap in the vfo that has to charge and discharge if the rit is used. The further off net the other station is  ,the  more voltage variation the varicap has to shift from tx to rx etc. I often use my calibrated ts590s to monitor and check my own neting calibration and to monitor my tx rf sent to air.  The one shot digital internal vfo is also available on this rig. It is quiet funny to watch it chase its self before settling to the vf frequency. Takes about 4 seconds obtain initial digital lock to the analogue vfo.

Regards Paul

name: Jamie
comments: I came to the party late and listened on 80 but heard nothing. Coming back to 40m I heard one side of a QSO between VK4PN and someone else.  I then picked up Mark VK2KI/P calling CQ.  His signal was strong but fading back into the static a little before coming back.  After making initial contact, at the end of Mark’s first over the fading was getting worse so I had one quick over and  sent 73.  While I could initially hear Mark’s final response it soon disappeared and I could barely tell if he had stopped sending or faded out completely.  Still happy to have at least one short QSL in the log.  Thanks Mark.
